title: How Logology automated $2,000 logo design into a $100 product and landed its first customer
summary: Dagobert Renouf explains how he and his designer wife turned a $2,000 custom logo service into a $100 automated questionnaire-to-logo product. He covers getting the first customer, when startups should invest in branding, and standing out in a crowded no-code market.

principles.text: Productize an expensive service by automating the expert's process so a price-constrained segment can afford it.
principles.quote: can we make the thing that we that you sell for 2 000 for like a week of work you know consulting can we make that cheap i mean not not cheap affordable you know at like 100 or 200 bucks

principles.text: Automate by copying how the expert actually works: ask discovery questions, then match to ideas.
principles.quote: we try to really copy how she works so usually the way she works is she's gonna ask questions uh from the client like what's your vision what are your values you know who's your target customer

principles.text: Build a deep, domain-specific catalog rather than generic assets, so output carries real meaning for each segment.
principles.quote: what we did in the past two and a half years is try to design a catalog of logos for every type of startup

principles.text: A product can be perfect for a few people who buy instantly; the hard part is extending that to everyone.
principles.quote: it can be very very good for a few people and then they just fall in love with it instantly and just buy it so now what's difficult is doing that with everyone

principles.text: Don't spend on a logo with zero customers; invest in branding once about 10-20 people love what you do.
principles.quote: if you have zero customers probably not time but like if you start to get a bit of traction like you found you know at least 10 or 20 people who really love what you do

principles.text: In crowded no-code markets, distinctive branding makes people pause instead of skipping, though copy and product still matter.
principles.quote: it just gives people uh a bit of like of a pause when they come to the website and instead of just skipping they're gonna check it out
